draft.title: Search + browse findability
draft.principle_summary: Findability sits between two channels, search and browse/navigation, that most users mix rather than choose between. Faceted filtering outperforms keyword search alone for structured catalogs, but only when facets stay legible: counts before applying, easy removal, no dead-end empty states. Zero-result and reformulation moments are the highest-risk points in the flow and need a concrete recovery path, not generic tips. Result scanning follows a top-left-weighted, F-shaped gaze pattern, so the highest-value differentiator per result belongs top-left and early, not buried after price.

sources.claim: Users split into search-dominant and link-dominant types; in task testing with a technical audience, 70 percent of users started a task by clicking a link and 30 percent started with search, because clicking a visible link is faster and easier than typing a query.
sources.source: Katz and Byrne 2003, cited in Nielsen Norman Group, "Converting Search into Navigation" and "Search Is Not Enough: Synergy Between Navigation and Search" (nngroup.com/articles/search-navigation, nngroup.com/articles/search-not-enough)

sources.claim: Hierarchical faceted search interfaces should avoid ever landing the user on an empty result set, should show item counts before a facet is applied, should support fluid alternation between narrowing and broadening a query, and should keep the user's current filter state visible and reversible at all times.
sources.source: Marti Hearst, "Design Recommendations for Hierarchical Faceted Search Interfaces", ACM SIGIR Workshop on Faceted Search, 2006 (flamenco.berkeley.edu/papers/faceted-workshop06.pdf)

sources.claim: Real-world information seeking rarely resolves in one query. Searchers gather relevant results bit by bit across a shifting series of queries and reformulations as each result read changes their sense of what they want ("berrypicking"), which is why a search flow needs to support easy reformulation, not just one committed query per result page.
sources.source: Marcia Bates, "The Design of Browsing and Berrypicking Techniques for the Online Search Interface", Online Review 13(5), 1989

sources.claim: On text-heavy, low-visual-hierarchy result and content pages, users scan in an F-shaped pattern: reading the first line fully, scanning a shorter second line, then dropping their gaze down the left edge. The pattern is a fallback that appears specifically where content lacks structure or entry points to guide the eye.
sources.source: Jakob Nielsen, "F-Shaped Pattern For Reading Web Content", Nielsen Norman Group, 2006 eye-tracking study, n=232 (nngroup.com/articles/f-shaped-pattern-reading-web-content)

sources.claim: An effective zero-results recovery page offers concrete next actions, spelling corrections, related category links, and popular or nearby items, not generic tips like "check your spelling" or "try broader terms", which are largely ignored. A large share of e-commerce sites still ship a dead-end zero-results page with no recovery path.
sources.source: Baymard Institute, "5 Proven UX Strategies For 'No Results' Pages" (baymard.com/blog/no-results-page)

sources.claim: Choice overload is a weak, non-replicating effect at the population level (meta-analysis d approx 0.02); the fix for hard-to-compare option sets is grouping and side-by-side comparability, not trimming the catalog.
sources.source: Solen's own PSYCHOLOGY.md law 11, cross-referenced here rather than restated

numbers_used: 70 percent link-first / 30 percent search-first (Katz and Byrne 2003)
n=232 in the 2006 NN/g F-pattern eye-tracking study
choice-overload meta-analysis d approx 0.02 (already sourced in PSYCHOLOGY.md, restated only as a cross-reference, not re-verified here)
draft.solen_current: RATIONALE.md has no findability or search/browse domain. Adjacent but non-overlapping material exists: line 71 covers single-select filters and Hick's law for decision latency (choice count, not findability mechanics); line 155 covers grouping/containment (visual structure of already-decided groups, not search); line 693 covers signifiers for clickability generally; line 705 covers progressive disclosure generally (filter sheets named as an existing practice, no mechanic attached); line 807 covers "no dead ends" as a generic copy law citing Yifrah, already the closest existing hook for a zero-results mechanic but not written for search specifically. PSYCHOLOGY.md law 11 (comparability-over-trimming, line in the 15-laws list) is the behavioral half: don't cap the option set, group into 3-5 labeled categories. Project memory (project_search_facts.md) holds the backend fact that /api/salons AND-combines filters and search is single-select by owner lock, but that is implementation, not a sourced UX layer. No doc anywhere states scanning order, facet-count discipline, or reformulation/zero-result recovery mechanics.
draft.gap: Missing domain. Solen has scattered fragments (dead-ends copy law, progressive disclosure, choice-comparability psychology) but nothing that ties them into a search-and-browse-specific mechanics layer: no rule for how many facets is too many, no rule for what a zero-Angebote-result state must contain, no rule for where the differentiating fact on a scannable result row belongs, and no acknowledgment that search and browse are parallel channels most users move between rather than a single mode to pick.
draft.proposed_addition:
DOMAIN: Findability (search + browse mechanics), new section for RATIONALE.md, target_anchor "new domain: findability". Suggested placement: immediately after the existing Domain 11 (enforcement) block, numbered by whatever the synthesis pass assigns next; content below, ready to paste.

Search and browse are not two competing modes users pick between, they are two channels most sessions mix: link-first behavior dominates when the path is visible (T2, Katz and Byrne 2003, cited by NN/g), search-first behavior dominates when it is not, and the same session often does both. This domain governs the mechanics UNDER Solen's existing search and Angebote-filter behavior (single-select owner lock, AND-combine backend, already project fact, not repeated here); it does not reopen either.

**Facet legibility over facet count (T2, Hearst 2006 design recommendations, converging with general faceted-search practice).** A facet set earns its keep by staying legible, not by covering every column the data has: show the result count before a facet is applied so the user is choosing an outcome, not guessing; make every applied facet visibly removable in one tap; never let a facet combination resolve to zero results without recovery (the empty-set-avoidance recommendation below). Mechanic for Solen: cap visible top-level Angebote facet chips to what fits one unscrolled row at the 375px floor (ground the exact count in the existing TabPill/filter-pill component's measured width, do not invent a number); anything beyond that goes behind a single "Mehr Filter" disclosure, which is already Solen's progressive-disclosure practice (RATIONALE.md line 705) newly given a search-specific trigger condition.

**Query reformulation is the normal path, not the failure path (T2, Bates 1989 berrypicking model).** Users rarely resolve intent in one query; they read a few results, then narrow or broaden. Mechanic: changing a facet or the search term must never force a full navigation reload that loses scroll position or the prior result set's context; the UI should read as adjusting a live view, not restarting a search. This is a perceptual/interaction requirement, independent of whatever the backend does to refetch.

**Zero-result and low-result states need a named recovery path, not a dead end (T3, Baymard Institute no-results research, directional; institute benchmarking, not peer-reviewed, so treat the specific percentages as industry-reported rather than re-verified here).** A zero-Angebote-result state must offer at least one concrete next action: relax the most restrictive active facet (name it: "Kein Ergebnis fuer X, Y anzeigen"), or surface the nearest adjacent category/city, never a bare "keine Ergebnisse" with no path forward. This is the search-specific instance of Solen's existing generic no-dead-ends copy law (RATIONALE.md line 807, Yifrah); the addition here is that search needs a STRUCTURAL recovery action (a tappable relax-filter control), not just recovery COPY.

**Result-row scanning is top-left-weighted (T2, Nielsen 2006 F-pattern eye-tracking, n=232, explicitly a fallback pattern that appears when a page lacks structure).** On an unstructured list this predicts where attention concentrates; Solen's cards are NOT unstructured (photo-led, named hierarchy per LOCKFILE card grammar), so the F-pattern does not override the existing card recipe, but it does set a placement rule for any NEW scannable text added to a result row: the single fact most likely to differentiate one result from its neighbors in a filtered list (the fact the user filtered ON, such as the matched service or the active promo) reads best placed early/top in the card's text block, not appended after price, because that is the zone gaze reaches first and most reliably before disengaging.

**Boundary.** This domain covers the PERCEPTUAL and INTERACTION mechanics of finding something (facet legibility, reformulation continuity, recovery structure, scan placement). It explicitly does NOT cover: which filters Solen offers, single-select vs multi-select policy, the AND-combine backend contract, or ranking/personalization logic, those are locked product/backend decisions living in project memory and fable-backend, not perceptual law, and none of them are reopened here. Choice-count and option-overload psychology stay in PSYCHOLOGY.md law 11 (comparability-over-trimming); this domain cross-references it rather than duplicating it; do not re-derive an overload argument here.

Taste-Lab probe design (for calibrating the facet-row-count and reformulation-continuity defaults against real Solen surfaces, since neither number above is locked): show two versions of the Angebote filter bar at 375px, one with the top-level facets fit to one unscrolled row plus a "Mehr Filter" disclosure, one with a second wrapped row of facets and no disclosure; ask which feels faster to scan, and separately time first-facet-tap latency in a moderated session. A second probe: apply a facet combination that yields zero results, show the relax-filter recovery action versus a bare empty state, and ask which one users would tap first without prompting. Both probes exist to calibrate the NUMBER (how many facets before disclosure), the DIRECTION (structural recovery beats copy-only recovery) is already T3-sourced above and does not need recalibration, only the Solen-specific threshold does.
draft.taste_lab_probe: Two-part probe. Probe 1 (facet-row-count threshold): at 375px width, compare the Angebote filter bar fit to one unscrolled row with a "Mehr Filter" disclosure against a version that wraps to a second row with no disclosure; measure first-facet-tap latency and ask which feels faster to scan. Probe 2 (recovery-path structure): apply a facet combination that yields zero results; compare a bare "keine Ergebnisse" empty state against one offering a tappable relax-the-most-restrictive-facet action; ask which the user would tap first, unprompted. Both calibrate Solen-specific numeric thresholds; the underlying directional claims (structural recovery beats copy-only, legible facets beat exhaustive facets) are already T2/T3-sourced and are not what the probe is testing.

verified.title: Search + browse findability

claim_verdicts.claim: Katz and Byrne 2003: 70% link-first / 30% search-first in task testing with a technical audience, cited by NN/G Converting Search into Navigation / Search Is Not Enough
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed live: NN/G's own pages (nngroup.com/articles/search-navigation) attribute this split to Katz and Byrne 2003. Real study, real number, correctly attributed as a secondary citation through NN/G rather than a primary-source read. T2 is honest for a single usability study reported via a secondary source, not inflated to T1.

claim_verdicts.claim: Hearst 2006, Design Recommendations for Hierarchical Faceted Search Interfaces, ACM SIGIR Workshop on Faceted Search: avoid empty result sets, show counts before applying, support narrow/broaden alternation, keep filter state visible and reversible
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed: real paper, published August 2006, hosted at flamenco.berkeley.edu/papers/faceted-workshop06.pdf (matches the draft's cited URL exactly), summarizing 13 years of Flamenco faceted-browsing research. Recommendations as paraphrased match what the paper is known for. T2 correct for a workshop paper synthesizing a research program, not a meta-analysis.

claim_verdicts.claim: Bates 1989, The Design of Browsing and Berrypicking Techniques for the Online Search Interface, Online Review 13(5): information seeking rarely resolves in one query, searchers iterate through reformulations
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed: real peer-reviewed article, Online Review 1989 vol 13 issue 5 pages 407-424, 414 citations as of 2014 tracking, foundational and still-cited berrypicking model. Description accurate. T2 correct.

claim_verdicts.claim: Nielsen 2006 F-Shaped Pattern eye-tracking study, n=232, users scan top-left-weighted on unstructured text-heavy pages
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed: NN/G's original 2006 eyetracking study recorded 232 users, matches the n=232 figure exactly, and NN/G's own later writing frames it as a pattern tied to low-structure content, matching the draft's caveat. Worth flagging as a residual risk rather than a refutation: independent eye-tracking work (EyeQuant and others) has since challenged how universal the F-pattern is and shown other scan shapes depending on layout, so the draft's own hedge (fallback pattern, does not override a structured card) is doing real work and should stay, not be dropped.

claim_verdicts.claim: Baymard Institute, 5 Proven UX Strategies For No Results Pages: effective recovery needs concrete next actions not generic tips; large share of e-commerce sites ship a dead-end zero-results page
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed: real Baymard article at that URL, current content describes roughly half of sites failing to give an effective no-results recovery path and lists concrete recovery strategies (alternative terms, clear messaging, related content), consistent with the draft's paraphrase. Baymard is a commercial UX benchmarking institute, not peer-reviewed, so T3 (directional, not academically verified) is the honest tier, correctly assigned, not inflated to T2/T1.

claim_verdicts.claim: Choice overload is a weak, non-replicating effect at the population level (meta-analysis d approx 0.02); fix is grouping/comparability, not catalog trimming, cross-referenced to Solen's own PSYCHOLOGY.md law 11
claim_verdicts.note: This is an internal cross-reference to an already-verified Solen doc, not a fresh external claim; the d approx 0.02 figure matches the myth screen's own prescribed substitute for the debunked jam-study narrative almost verbatim (myth screen: 'overload needs moderators; fix comparability (d~0.02)'), so it is correctly using the approved replacement language rather than the banned pop-stat. Per task instructions this entry is not re-verified here, only checked for consistency with the myth screen, and it is consistent.

verified.residual_risks:
All five external sources (Katz and Byrne 2003, Hearst 2006, Bates 1989, Nielsen F-pattern 2006, Baymard no-results) checked out as real, correctly described, and honestly tiered (T2 for the academic/NN/G studies, T3 for the commercial Baymard benchmark). No myth-table numbers appear and the one internal cross-reference (choice-overload d approx 0.02) matches the myth screen's own approved substitute language rather than the banned jam-study narrative, so nothing needed cutting.

Two things for the owner to weigh, not claim failures: (1) the F-pattern citation is real but the pattern itself has been challenged by later independent eye-tracking work as not universal across layouts, the verified_addition already hedges this in-line, flagging it here so it does not get quietly strengthened into a hard rule in a later pass. (2) The facet-row-count number and the exact zero-result relax-filter copy are both explicitly left uncalibrated (Taste-Lab probe candidates), consistent with the "don't invent numbers" rule, this is a QUESTIONS.md candidate once the synthesis pass numbers the domain, not something to lock from this draft alone. Neither risk blocks merging the addition, both are calibration/monitoring items.
